parts.note: Michael Balfe's best-known opera is titled after a girl from a central European land, and this word completes its title

explanation.surface: Someone's daughter or sweetheart, belonging to a man named Balfe.
explanation.walkthrough: Balfe was an Irish composer whose opera 'The Bohemian Girl' (1843) was hugely popular; the clue asks for the word that completes its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Balfe's opera names its heroine as a girl from Bohemia, so the adjective fills the gap.

parts.note: a bra is the garment that holds the bust up
HMS, His or Her Majesty's Ship, prefixes the name of a British warship

explanation.surface: A naval vessel blowing up, with a conductor looking on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust-up' reads as a quarrel or explosion, but it is a garment that keeps the bust up.
explanation.definitionFit: Johannes Brahms was a great German composer, and maestro is a title for a master of music.

parts.note: the timer with two glass bulbs is pinched narrow in the middle, so it has a waist, and it measures time

explanation.surface: A grumble that something is pointless, a waste of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waist' sounds like 'waste', turning a complaint into a description of the narrow-middled sand timer.
explanation.definitionFit: The sand timer has two bulbs joined at a narrow neck like a waist, and it marks a fixed span of time.

parts.note: George Moore wrote an 1885 novel called 'A ... Wife', about the wife of a travelling actor; this word fills the gap

explanation.surface: A question about the spouse of a man called Moore.
explanation.walkthrough: George Moore's novel 'A Mummer's Wife' supplies the answer: the clue drops the word before 'wife'. Mummers are actors in traditional folk plays.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of George Moore's novel names the heroine as a strolling player's spouse, so the plural noun completes the reference.

parts.note: in Dickens's David Copperfield the hero's second wife is Miss Wickfield

explanation.surface: A question about the spouse of a man called David.
explanation.walkthrough: The David is Dickens's David Copperfield, whose second wife is Agnes Wickfield; the biblical David's wives are a false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Dickens novel the narrator marries Agnes Wickfield after his first wife Dora dies.

clue.text: A marked man, Edward got the wind up

parts.note: a scar is the mark that leaves a man marked
Ed is a short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: Edward, a man singled out as a target, took fright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A marked man' suggests someone targeted, but it stands for the mark itself. To 'get the wind up' is British slang for becoming frightened.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting the wind up is an informal idiom for becoming frightened or alarmed.

clue.text: Clay-spattered fellow at the scene of the boar-hunt

indicators.note: the letters of the word clay are splashed about into a new order

parts.note: a don is a fellow of a university college

explanation.surface: A muddy man standing where hunters chased a wild boar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spattered' rearranges CLAY into CALY. The boar-hunt is the Calydonian Boar Hunt of Greek legend, set in the city of Calydon.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek myth places the hunt for the monstrous boar sent by Artemis at the city of Calydon in Aetolia.

parts.note: Wordsworth lived from 1813 at a house in the Lake District named after a nearby lake and village, called ... Mount

explanation.surface: A peak celebrated in English verse, like a poets' Parnassus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' suggests a mountain, but Rydal Mount is the house near Ambleside where Wordsworth lived for most of his life.
explanation.definitionFit: Rydal Mount was William Wordsworth's home in the Lake District from 1813 until his death in 1850.

clue.text: Airy castle for a light sleeper?

definitions.text: Airy castle for a light sleeper?

parts.words: Airy castle for a light sleeper?
parts.note: a castle in the air is a fanciful hope, the kind dreamt up while awake by someone only half asleep

explanation.surface: A breezy fortress suitable for someone who wakes easily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Airy castle' is a castle in the air, a fantasy; the 'light sleeper' is someone dreaming while awake rather than one who wakes easily.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverie is a pleasant fantasy indulged while awake, a castle in the air built by a waking dreamer.

clue.text: She at an all-time low coming up dramatically. Richard

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue the word is written upwards, so it is read from the bottom

parts.note: a nadir is the lowest point ever reached

explanation.surface: A woman at her lowest ebb recovers in theatrical style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' turns NADIR into RIDAN below SHE. Richard Brinsley Sheridan was the Irish playwright of The Rivals, hence 'dramatically'.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Brinsley Sheridan was the eighteenth-century dramatist who wrote The School for Scandal.

clue.text: When the driver, changing gear, may take a back seat

definitions.text: When the driver, changing gear, may take a back seat

parts.words: When the driver, changing gear, may take a back seat
parts.note: a bus driver on his day off, in his own clothes rather than uniform, rides as a passenger on someone else's bus

explanation.surface: A motorist shifting gears and letting someone else steer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing gear' means changing clothes out of uniform, not using the gearbox. The phrase means leisure spent doing what one does at work.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes time off spent doing much the same as one's usual job, like a driver riding a bus on his day off.

parts.note: bars of iron that draw metal towards them by attraction

explanation.surface: A coupling rod on a cart or railway wagon, called a drawbar.
explanation.walkthrough: A drawbar is a coupling on a vehicle; split, 'draw' and 'bars' describe bar-shaped objects that attract iron.
explanation.definitionFit: Bar-shaped lodestones attract or draw iron filings, so they are bars that draw.

definitions.meaning: a riddle is a coarse sieve, and to riddle something is to pierce it full of holes, so this is one that makes things holey
the Sphinx of Greek legend set a puzzle to travellers and killed those who failed

explanation.surface: An exclamation, 'Holy Sphinx!', in the style of a comic-book catchphrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holey' looks like a misspelt 'holy' in an oath; it points to a riddle, the sieve full of holes.
explanation.definitionFit: One who riddles fills things with holes or sifts with a sieve, and the Sphinx posed a famous puzzle to Oedipus.

parts.note: the word a hopeful candidate longs to hear is the result 'pass', and a shibboleth is a test word letting someone through

explanation.surface: The catchphrase or creed of a student optimistic about an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: A shibboleth is a test word that admits insiders (from Judges 12); the examinee's 'word' is the one result they hope for.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret test word that lets you through a guarded point, as a shibboleth did, and also the word 'pass' that a candidate hopes for.

indicators.note: something in trouble is in disorder, so these letters are thrown into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A gift made to England in its hour of need.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' rearranges the eight letters of TO ALBION. Albion is a poetic name for Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblation is a religious gift presented to God, especially bread and wine at the Eucharist.

clue.text: First class hair-do back in the country

indicators.note: the two pieces together are read from right to left

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, its figure written as the letter I
a bun is hair wound into a knot at the back of the head

explanation.surface: A top-quality hairstyle making a comeback out in the provinces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns A1 plus BUN into NUBIA; 'the country' looks like rural parts but is the ancient land on the Nile.
explanation.definitionFit: Nubia is the historic land along the Nile south of Egypt, an ancient kingdom and region.

clue.text: It's not for drinking, except perhaps in Somerset

definitions.text: It's not for drinking, except perhaps in Somerset

parts.words: It's not for drinking, except perhaps in Somerset
parts.note: the water of a tub is not drunk, but the spa town in Somerset serves its mineral spring water in the Pump Room

explanation.surface: A warning about water unfit to drink, with an exception in one English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is a spa town in Somerset, a county of south-west England, where visitors drink the hot spring water in the Pump Room.
explanation.definitionFit: Used tub water is not drunk, while the spa waters of the city of Bath have been drunk for health since Roman times.

clue.text: It had an old man too in Ruskin

definitions.text: It had an old man too in Ruskin

parts.words: It had an old man too in Ruskin
parts.note: John Ruskin lived at Brantwood beside a Lake District water overlooked by a fell nicknamed the Old Man

explanation.surface: A remark that Ruskin's world also contained an elderly gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruskin's home Brantwood stands on Coniston Water, above which rises the fell called the Old Man of Coniston; 'in Ruskin's day' is the sense of 'in Ruskin'.
explanation.definitionFit: The village and lake where Ruskin lived lie beneath the mountain known as the Old Man of Coniston.

clue.text: Watering-place where the sands aren't overcrowded

definitions.text: Watering-place where the sands aren't overcrowded

parts.words: Watering-place where the sands aren't overcrowded
parts.note: a seaside resort is a watering-place with busy sands, but this one is a spring alone in a desert of empty sand

explanation.surface: A quiet seaside resort with uncrowded beaches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watering-place' and 'sands' suggest a British seaside resort; the sands are desert and the watering-place a fertile spot with water.
explanation.definitionFit: A fertile spot in a desert where water is found, surrounded by empty sands.

definitions.meaning: brief moments of time, sixtieths of a minute, pass very quickly
in a duel or boxing match, the attendants who back up each fighter

explanation.surface: Backers whose loyalty does not last long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short-lived' stands for the tiny units of time; 'supporters' are the attendants of a duellist or boxer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sixtieths of a minute are brief spans of time, and a duellist's or boxer's attendants are called by the same plural word.

parts.note: laying linoleum means trimming it, and prints are made from blocks of linoleum carved by an artist

explanation.surface: Admiring the craftsmanship of a newly laid floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitting lino means cutting it, but the artistic sense is a print taken from a carved block of linoleum.
explanation.definitionFit: Prints made by carving a design into linoleum and inking it are named for the cutting of the floor covering.

definitions.meaning: a full-petalled variety of rose shares its name with the vegetable
greens are leafy vegetables such as kale and savoy

explanation.surface: A colour description, a rosy green shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a colour or a past tense; it is the cabbage rose, Rosa centifolia.
explanation.definitionFit: The cabbage rose is a densely petalled variety, and the leafy brassica is a typical green vegetable.

parts.note: a degree is a step or rank, and being placed on a scale of steps means being ranked

explanation.surface: Awarded a university qualification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Degree' suggests a university award, but it is a grade or step on a scale.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ranked at a particular level or step on a scale, as eggs or students are sorted by quality.

parts.note: a still is an apparatus for distilling spirits, and an unlicensed one is banned by law

explanation.surface: Something that remains banned to this day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' reads as 'yet', but it is the distilling apparatus: an illicit still makes moonshine.
explanation.definitionFit: Illegal or forbidden by law, the standard phrase for an unlicensed spirit distillery.

clue.text: Dilke, a broken man, was popular

indicators.note: the name Dilke is smashed apart and reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A ruined politician named Dilke was once well loved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges DILKE. Sir Charles Dilke was a Victorian politician ruined by a divorce scandal in 1886, so 'a broken man' fits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Being well thought of by people means being popular.

parts.note: Fair Rosamond, mistress of Henry II, was kept in a secluded retreat at Woodstock known as Rosamond's Bower

explanation.surface: An instruction to humble a woman called Rosamond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in her place' means to snub; here it means to enclose her in her bower, Rosamond's Bower at Woodstock, from English legend.
explanation.definitionFit: To enclose in a leafy shelter or arbour, as Fair Rosamond was in the bower Henry II built for her.

parts.note: a Scottish town shares its name with the earl whose marble sculptures from the Parthenon are in the British Museum

explanation.surface: A Scottish town built of marble.
explanation.walkthrough: A burgh is a Scottish town; 'marmoreal' (of marble) points to the Elgin Marbles taken from Athens by Lord Elgin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moray town shares its name with the earl whose name is attached to the Parthenon marbles.

clue.text: A gift may be assumed to be

definitions.text: A gift may be assumed to be

parts.words: A gift may be assumed to be
parts.note: a gift is something granted, and the phrase also means assumed without question

explanation.surface: A thought on what can be supposed about a present.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means 'assumed true without question', and a gift is literally 'taken', 'for' something 'granted'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means accepted as true without question, while a gift is literally received as something bestowed.

parts.note: a habit is a garment such as a monk's robe, and this person wears no clothes at all

explanation.surface: Someone who does not usually do something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' reads as custom, but it is clothing such as a monk's habit or riding habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A naturist goes unclothed, so wears no garment of any kind.

clue.text: As the good that dead men did, said Antony

definitions.text: As the good that dead men did, said Antony

parts.words: As the good that dead men did, said Antony
parts.note: Mark Antony's funeral speech says the evil men do lives after them while the good is buried with their bones

explanation.surface: A quotation attributed to Antony about the good deeds of the dead.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Act 3: 'The evil that men do lives after them; the good is oft interred with their bones.'
explanation.definitionFit: In Mark Antony's oration the good deeds of the dead are said to be buried along with their bones.
